target_name: Rozwój ekologicznych i efektywnych systemów ciepłowniczych
description: W 2018 r. kryterium systemu efektywnego energetycznie spełnia tylko ok. 20% spośród systemów ciepłowniczych lub chłodniczych, które dostarczają ok. 85% ogólnego wolumenu ciepła systemowego w kraju. Pokrycie potrzeb cieplnych powinno odbywać się przede wszystkim poprzez wykorzystanie ciepła sieciowego. Zapewnia to wysoką efektywność wykorzystania surowca, poprawia komfort życia obywateli i ogranicza problem niskiej emisji. Jeśli przyłączenie do sieci ciepłowniczej nie jest możliwe, należy dążyć do wykorzystania źródeł indywidualnych o możliwie najniższej emisyjności.
progress: Wdrożono mechanizm obowiązkowego raportowania danych dotyczących efektywnego systemu ciepłowniczego. Dotychczas istniejące w Polsce mechanizmy bazowały na danych dotyczących przedsiębiorstwa, a system co do zasady nie był podstawowym podmiotem analizy. Wprowadzone zostały zmiany w legislacji mające uatrakcyjnić wykorzystywanie źródeł odnawialnych w ciepłownictwie systemowym, ponadto uruchomiono szereg mechanizmów wsparcia inwestycyjnego.
expected_impact: Wdrożono mechanizm obowiązkowego raportowania danych dotyczących efektywnego systemu ciepłowniczego. target_name: Improving energy and material efficiency according to the "energy efficiency first" principle in all sectors
description: General objective and focus for all sectors as energy and material efficiency is the first and key measure for the transition to a climate-neutral society. Reducing consumption of energy and other natural resources is therefore crucial.
progress: Within this, general objective, concrete quantitative sector targets and indicators for progress evaluation are set in the NECP 2024. Some are listed within this table, while others (renovation of 3% of the total floor area of public buildings; EEOS and alternative measures) are presented in other tables of this reporting.

target_name: In 2030, final energy use will be lower than 50,2 TWh (4.320 ktoe)
description: The main national target in the area of energy efficiency is set in line with the recommendations of EC to apply the gap filling mechanism of 4.32 Mtoe to support the achievement of more ambitious target of reducing EU final energy consumption by 11.7% by 2030, compared to the projected energy use for 2030. Slovenia set the target at the level of FEC.
progress: In 2023, the final energy use was 52.2 TWh (4,491 ktoe). In comparison to 2022 it decreased by 5%. In comparison to 2005 the final energy use decreased by 12%. The indicative annual target of 55.5 TWh (4,772 ktoe) was achieved.
expected_impact: The achievement of the target will contribute to the reduction of GHG emissions and thus to the transition into the climate-neutrality.

target_name: Reduction of final energy use in buildings by 15% by 2030 compared to 2020
description: The objective is to reduce the final energy use in buildings by implementation of energy efficiency measures to achieve the reduction of 15% by 2030 in comparison to 2020.
progress:
"In 2023, the final energy use in buildings was 3.8% lower than in 2020. In households it decreased by 4.7% and in services by 1.6%. In 2022 there was a change in the statistical methodology for the service sector, which is now not anymore treated as the residual in the energy balance. The final energy use in 2023 was thus a little bit lagging behind the indicative target for this year (a reduction of 4.5%, calculated using a linear extrapolation). By 2030, the final energy use in buildings must decrease by another 11.2 percentage points.
Compared to 2022 the final energy use was lower by 0.8%. In households a new trend of increased electricity use in households with self-supply was observed. Compared to 2005 the energy use was 23% lower."
expected_impact: The achievement of the target will contribute to the reduction of GHG emissions and thus to the transition into the climate-neutrality.

target_name: Reduction of final energy use in the public sector by 1.9% annually compared to 2021
description: The objective is to reduce the final energy use in the public sector by implementation of energy efficiency measures to achieve the annual reduction of 1.9% in comparison to 2021.
progress: The reduction is not yet being monitored. At the moment, an inventory of all public buildings and an assessment of final energy use in the public sector in the base year are  being prepared.
expected_impact: The achievement of the target will contribute to the reduction of GHG emissions and thus to the transition into the climate-neutrality.

description:
In its Policy Statement on Geothermal Energy for a Circular Economy, the Government outlined the scope of a strategy for the greater deployment of geothermal energy in support of Ireland’s climate goals, in particular the decarbonisation of heating and cooling. The scope of the strategy is aligned with the energy efficiency dimension of the energy union. To manage peak seasonal loads on the electricity grid from the electrification of heating, the 
strategy will examine targets for the optimal deployment of ground-source heat pumps 
relative to air-source heat pumps and promote the use of geothermal storage and re-use of 
heat to balance heating and cooling loads. Geothermal energy has been identified as a potentially significant source of heat for district heating networks and can play a role in balancing diverse loads in local networks, particularly those integrating industrial processes.
progress:
DECC has commenced work on the detailed research, design and stress testing of the proposed regulatory approach. DECC will continue to engage with stakeholders in that work, including industry and the Geothermal Energy Advisory Group. The members of the advisory group are drawn from the environmental, geoscientific, industry and social pillars, as well as Government Departments and regulators. Following engagement with stakeholders DECC will prepare a General Scheme of a Bill during 2025 to provide the necessary legislative basis for the regulatory framework.

Within the scope of the strategy outlined in the policy statement, DECC is continuing to develop the National Geothermal Database, provide guidance for public sector organisations in assessing geothermal energy to meet climate targets, and support the GEMINI project to inter alia deliver demonstration projects for both deep and shallow geothermal systems. DECC continues to assess the economic case for setting targets for the deployment of geothermal energy.
expected_impact: N/A. To date, no targets have been set.

description:
In the public sector, the SEAI has been operating a Pathfinder programme providing opportunities for public sector bodies to implement pilot retrofit projects. 
Through the Pathfinder projects, public bodies learn how to replicate retrofit successfully across their wider building estates.
progress:
The SEAI Pathfinder Programme, co-funded with building portfolio owners, provides capital funding for implementing building retrofit approaches in the public sector. The programme is targeted particularly at public sector portfolio managers, where retrofit and decarbonisation options. New Programme principles are proposed and policy recommendations made. Activity can be coordinated centrally and is aimed at testing building retrofit approaches and developing a model that can be replicated and scaled across the wider public sector. 
SEAI has carried out a review of this programme; the learnings of the review will continue to inform decision-making on retrofit and decarbonisation options.  New Programme principles are proposed and policy recommendations made.

description: The Plan sets out targets for the significant improvement of the energy efficiency of our building stock with a target of the equivalent of 500,000 existing buildings to be retrofitted to a B2 Building Energy Rating or cost optimal by 2030.
progress:
In the period 2019- 2024, over 201,000 home upgrades have been supported under SEAI and Local authority retrofit schemes. Of this, over 65,000 were to a B2 level.


Significant demand for the SEAI schemes continued in 2024 with almost 70,000 applications for grant support received– up 4% on 2023. In 2023, grant support was provided for almost 48,000 upgrades. In 2024, it was almost 54,000.  There was 21,817 B2 upgrades completed which is up 24% on 2023 and 105% of 2024 target.

The system is ramping up towards delivering an average of 75,000 homes per year for the second half of the decade.
expected_impact: Equivalent of 120,000 dwellings retrofitted to BER B2 cost optimal and 45,000 existing dwellings using heat pumps by 2025.

description: All new dwellings will be built to NZEB standard from 1 November 2019. All new "Buildings other than dwellings" are built to NZEB from 1st Jan 2019.
expected_impact: New homes will be 70% more energy efficient and will emit 70% less carbon dioxide than 2005 performance levels. buildings should be less energy intensive and therefore cheaper to run than less efficient buildings. Other impacts may be improved air quality and comfort.

description: The CAP commits to the publication of a National Heat Policy Statement that will draw on the evidence of the National Heat Study and set out the overarching approach to decarbonising the heat sector in Ireland.
progress: In order to finalise the Strategic Environmental Assessment on the draft Heat Policy Statement, a public consultation will be undertaken. Following completion of public consultation process, the draft Policy Statement will be submitted to Government for approval.
expected_impact: The National Heat Policy Statement will set out the overarching approach to decarbonising the heat sector in Ireland.

description: Phase 2 of the social housing retrofit programme to bring dwellings to a B2 equivalent BER.
progress:
In 2024, 2,634 social homes were retrofitted by Local Authorities. Heat Pumps were installed on 2,393 of these properties representing 90.85% installation of heat pumps on those LA homes retrofitted.

Since the programme commenced in 2021, 8,400 dwellings have been retrofitted to B2/Cost Optimal levels with heat pumps installed in 7,256 homes.
expected_impact: Continue rollout of Social Housing National Retrofitting Programme with retrofitted properties required to reach a minimum BER B2 and incorporating heat pump deployment targets ensuring 36,500 LA owned homes are retrofit to 2030.

description:
The Heat and Built Environment Taskforce (HBET) was established in 2023 to ensure a coordinated approach to the accelerated implementation of climate actions designed to deliver energy-efficient buildings heated through renewable sources.

The Taskforce oversees the development and delivery of policies from across Government Departments and Agencies to ensure they are aligned and manages risks to delivery.

HBET members include senior officials from Government Departments and Agencies responsible for delivering energy-use optimisation in Ireland’s building stock, in line with the Climate Action Plan.

The HBET Focus Group acts on cross-cutting issues arising in Working Groups and serves as an advisory and escalation forum.

Seven Working Groups report to the Taskforce on:

•	Industrial Heat Decarbonisation
•	Commercial Built Environment
•	Public Sector Heat and Built Environment
•	Residential Retrofit
•	Biomethane
•	District Heating 
•	Unallocated Savings
progress:
The Heat and Built Environment Taskforce (HBET) has met thirteen times since its inception. The Minister for Environment, Climate and Communications has attended the majority of HBET meetings. 

The HBET has prepared an updated Implementation Plan for 2025 to be reported on quarterly.

The HBET is in the process of revising its operation and has produced a progress report in relation to actions up to 2024.

description: A shift to alternative heating sources for residential heating is also set out in the Plan, with a target of 680,000 heat pumps installed over the period 2021-2030, with 400,000 of these in existing dwellings.
progress:
In the period 2019 to end January 2025 almost 14,500 heat pumps have been installed under the SEAI energy efficiency upgrade schemes.

In addition, most recent figures from Dept of Housing, Local Government and Heritage show that in the period 2021-24 there were a further 7,256 heat pumps installed under the Local Authority Energy Efficiency Retrofit Programme.

This totals almost 21,750 heat pumps delivered across both SEAI and Local authority Schemes and is 48.3% of 2025 target and 5.4% of 2030 target.
expected_impact: Equivalent of 120,000 dwellings retrofitted to BER B2 cost optimal and 45,000 existing dwellings using heat pumps by 2025.

description: 50% energy efficiency and 51% emission reduction targets by 2030.
progress:
A Public Sector Building Register is being developed as part of an enhanced Monitoring and Reporting (M&R) System, managed by the SEAI. This enhanced M&R system will provide important insights into which buildings are generating the most emissions and will help to prioritise and sequence capital investments for decarbonisation strategies across the sector. 

Achievements in 2022 (the most recent data available) include 4,627GWh annual primary energy savings,32.5% energy efficiency improvement 3.9% fossil CO2 emission reduction, and €327m energy spend savings for the sector.

description: With respect to renewable transport fuels, CAP maintains previous commitments to increase the renewable biofuel content of motor fuels through an annual increase in the rate of the Renewable Transport Fuel Obligation, such that an E10:B20 equivalent is reached by 2030
progress: In 2024, the RTFO delivered a 9% ethanol blend in petrol and a 10.2% HVO/biodiesel blend in diesel, on track to meet the CAP 2025 interim targets of E10/B12. Regulations enacted in 2023 introduced a minimum blend of 5.5% ethanol in petrol.
expected_impact: Modelling analysis projects a saving of 1.08 MtCO2eq by 2030 from the CAP target of E10/B20 by 2030.

description: Progressively phase out oil and gas boilers in existing dwellings through a combination of incentives, information, and regulatory measures and the development of a Roadmap for the Phase Out of Fossil Fuel Heating Systems.
progress:
In addition to amendments made to the building regulations to end the installation of fossil fuel boilers in both new and existing residential buildings, a roadmap is being developed for the phase out of fossil fuel heating systems.

The roadmap will be informed by international experience, and will produce a timeline of key actions and implementation measures.

The roadmap will be aligned with the National Building Renovation Plan required by under the Energy Performance in Building Directive (EPBD).
expected_impact: The roadmap to phase out fossil fuel heating systems will set out a suite of policies and actions to phase out fossil fuel heating systems by 2040.

description: Effectively ban the installation of oil boilers from 2022 and the installation of gas boilers from 2025 in all new dwellings through the introduction of new regulatory standards for home heating systems. Progressively phase out oil and gas boilers in existing dwellings through a combination of incentives, information, and regulatory measures.
progress:
Fossil fuel heating systems have been effectively phased out as the main heating system in new dwellings, through progressive improvements in the Building Regulations, and replaced by renewable heating systems such as air source heat pumps.

Amendment of regulations to effectively 
ban fossil fuel boilers in existing dwellings undergoing major renovation where practical to achieve a post-works cost-optimal level BER of A3. Amendment is to be introduced and effective by end of 2025.
expected_impact:
97% of space heating systems installed in new dwellings completed in 2024 were using electricity as fuel.

The amendment of Cost-optimal level for major renovations from B2 to A3 could potentially lead to an increase of up to 40% in CO2 emissions savings for major renovations. This amendment supports the CAP targets of retrofitting 500,000 dwellings to B2 by 2030 and 400,000 dwellings using a heat pump by 2030.

description: Αn objective is set for the annual energy renovation of a total floor area of the thermal zone of central public administration buildings equal to 5 400 square meters, representing 3% of the total floor area in line with Article 5 of the EED
expected_impact: The objective is fulfilled with the renovation of the Hellenic Parliament building. The renovation was completed in 2023.

description: Hungary's final energy consumption should not exceed 740 PJ in 2030.
progress: It primarily relies on strengthening energy-efficiency measures, modernizing the energy performance of the building stock and industry, and encouraging end-user energy savings (support schemes, preferential financing, and regulatory incentives). In addition, increasing the share of renewable energy sources, electrifying energy carriers, reducing emissions and energy demand in the transport sector (public transport and electromobility), and shaping consumer awareness together contribute to ensuring that final energy consumption remains below the defined level by 2030.
expected_impact: Keeping final energy consumption below 740 PJ contributes to reducing greenhouse gas emissions, lowering dependence on imported energy carriers and strengthening security of supply, and in the longer term it may reduce energy costs for households and businesses. It also стимулиates energy-efficiency investments and innovation, improving the economy’s competitiveness and supporting the transition toward an economic structure with lower carbon emissions.

target_name: Minimum of cumulative final energy savings
description: The cumulative final energy savings target is set at 336.3 PJ. Based on the increase of the indicative energy savings target provided for in the Energy Efficiency Directive (EU) 2023/1791, Hungary should achieve cumulative final energy savings of 484.6 PJ by 2030. Achieving the indicative cumulative energy savings target is a major challenge in all areas and its feasibility is under review.
progress: Achieving the target is primarily ensured by energy renovations of the building stock (residential and public buildings), modernization of heating and cooling systems, increasing the share of renewable energy sources, the rollout of energy management and smart metering systems, the energy efficiency obligation scheme, and the provision of support and tax incentives—complemented by improvements in public lighting and the transport sector (public transport and electromobility).
expected_impact: The set cumulative final energy savings target contributes to reducing energy consumption and greenhouse gas emissions, lowers import dependence, and improves security of supply and households’ energy costs. In addition, it boosts energy-efficiency investments, encourages innovation and the creation of green jobs, thereby strengthening the economy’s competitiveness.

target_name: Energy use of residential building stock compared to 2018-2020 average
description: Hungary's target is to achieve energy savings of at least 20% in the energy use of its residential building stock by 2030, based on the average of the 2018-2020 reference years.
progress: To achieve at least a 20% reduction in energy use in residential buildings, Hungary can primarily rely on promoting building energy renovations (thermal insulation, window and door replacement, modernization of building services systems, and smart controls), as well as replacing fossil-based heating systems with modern, energy-efficient and renewable-based solutions (heat pumps, modern district heating, biomass, and solar energy). Progress toward the target is supported through grant schemes and preferential financing, targeted measures focusing on vulnerable households, and instruments under the energy efficiency obligation scheme.
expected_impact: Reducing the energy consumption of the residential building stock by at least 20% would significantly lower households’ utility costs, reduce dependence on energy imports, and contribute to cutting greenhouse gas emissions. It would also stimulate investment in the construction and energy sectors, support the creation of new jobs, and improve the comfort and value of residential buildings.

target_name: Energy consumption of public building stock compared to 2018-2020 average
description: The target is to achieve an 18% reduction in energy use in public buildings by 2030, based on the average of the 2018-2020 reference years.
progress: To achieve an 18% reduction in energy consumption in public buildings, Hungary prioritizes energy renovations of the public building stock (thermal insulation, replacement of windows and doors, modernization of heating, cooling and ventilation systems, lighting upgrades, and the installation of building management systems), as well as the integration of renewable energy sources (e.g., solar panels and heat pumps). Reaching the target is supported by programs financed from national and EU funds, energy efficiency obligation schemes, energy performance contracting (EPC) arrangements, and regulatory and institutional measures that strengthen the exemplary role of the public sector.
expected_impact: Reducing energy consumption in public buildings by 18% lowers the public sector’s energy costs, reduces pressures on the state budget, and contributes to cutting greenhouse gas emissions and dependence on energy imports. It also improves the buildings’ comfort and technical condition, strengthens the public sector’s exemplary role, and can encourage energy-efficiency investments in the private sector as well.

description: Our goal is for the rate of GDP growth to increasingly exceed the rate of growth in energy use, i.e. for the final energy intensity of GDP to improve, falling below 0.429 toe/million HUF by 2030. This would represent a reduction of 18% compared to 2021.
progress: To reduce GDP final energy intensity, Hungary relies on strengthening energy-efficiency investments, modernizing technologies in the industrial and services sectors, reducing energy demand in the building and transport sectors, and promoting the uptake of digitalization and energy management systems. Achieving the target is supported by subsidy and tax incentives, green financing instruments, strengthened innovation and R&D activities, and the expansion of higher value-added, less energy-intensive economic sectors.
expected_impact: Reducing GDP final energy intensity by 18% means that economic growth is achieved with lower energy use and lower greenhouse gas emissions, thereby reducing dependence on energy imports and strengthening security of supply. It also encourages the adoption of more efficient technologies and innovative solutions, boosts businesses’ competitiveness, and supports the development of an economic structure with lower carbon intensity.
